title: English Vocabulary 3 · Units 67–68
description: Curated B2 spoken discourse markers and formal written linkers for coherent communication, including register and discourse-function contrasts.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal study. Vocabulary targets follow source topics and exercise vocabulary; all teaching examples and notes are newly written, and original exercises, extended passages and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Complete study sections, dialogue illustrations, common-mistake note, exercises 67.1–67.4 and 68.1–68.4, and relevant answer-key entries checked for vocabulary, discourse function and usage.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA is given for shorter expressions when reliable. Longer or highly context-dependent expressions may have empty IPA instead of uncertain transcriptions; connected speech and regional variants are not exhaustively represented.
audit.languagePolicy: All content is in English except Brazilian Portuguese translations under pt.

units.title: Unit 67 — Discourse markers in spoken English
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 67. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Recognise discourse markers that organise turns and stages of an informal conversation.
Use hesitation, clarification and afterthought markers without changing the core meaning of a message.
Signal suggestions, interruptions, explanations, contrasts and topic changes naturally.
Identify common markers in rapid speech and avoid overusing them.

items.example: She uses discourse markers to keep her explanation clear.
items.note: A word or phrase that organises, comments on, or frames speech rather than adding its main factual content.

items.example: Well, I live near the city, but not in the centre.
items.note: Often marks a reply that is not a straightforward yes or no; may also restart an explanation.

items.example: Right, we have finished the introduction, so let us move on.
items.note: Used to signal a new stage or acknowledge that the previous point is settled; not the adjective meaning correct.

items.example: OK, does everyone understand the next step?
items.note: A spoken organising signal similar to right; it can begin a new activity or invite acknowledgement.

items.example: Now, we need to decide who will present the results.
items.note: In this context, signals a transition or new instruction rather than simply the present time.

items.example: So, shall we arrange another meeting for Friday?
items.note: Can move a conversation forward, reopen a topic or lead into a proposed next step.

items.example: Good, that covers everything we needed to discuss.
items.note: As a discourse marker, acknowledges progress or agreement and can help close a meeting.

items.example: Well then, what would you like to ask about the project?
items.note: Used to direct a conversation towards its next topic or activity.

items.example: Now then, I would like everyone to look at the diagram.
items.note: Often said by a teacher, presenter or another person guiding the conversation.

items.example: Fine, I will send you the updated agenda this afternoon.
items.note: A conversational signal of agreement, often used before bringing an exchange to a close.

items.example: Great, I will see you at the station tomorrow.
items.note: Friendly positive acknowledgement; often helps end an arrangement or exchange.

items.pt: onde eu estava mesmo?; onde eu tinha parado?
items.example: Where was I? Oh yes, I was explaining how the test failed.
items.note: A natural way to recover your place in a story or explanation after an interruption.

items.pt: veja bem; por outro lado; pensando bem
items.example: The flat is expensive. Mind you, it is right next to the station.
items.note: Adds a qualification or afterthought, often contrasting with what has just been said.

items.example: Let me see, I think I saved the document yesterday.
items.note: Gives the speaker time to remember, decide or locate information.

items.example: Listen, why don't we ask the technician to check it?
items.note: At the beginning of a turn, calls attention to an important point or proposal; can sound forceful.

items.example: Look, we can solve this without changing the entire design.
items.note: Directs attention to a point or suggestion; may be firm depending on tone.

items.example: Hang on, I have not finished explaining the first issue.
items.note: Stops or delays an interruption; informal, and also used to ask someone to wait.

items.pt: espere um pouco; só um instante
items.example: Hold on, I need to check one detail before you continue.
items.note: Close to hang on in this context; can interrupt politely or insistently according to intonation.

items.example: I cannot approve the purchase. You see, the budget is already fixed.
items.note: Introduces background or an explanation expected to make the previous statement clearer.

items.example: He was, you know, a little nervous about speaking in public.
items.note: Can fill a pause or seek shared understanding; excessive repetition makes speech less clear.

items.pt: meio que; mais ou menos; uma espécie de
items.example: The interface is sort of confusing until you practise with it.
items.note: Informal hedging or approximation; may soften a description or show uncertainty.

items.pt: meio que; mais ou menos; uma espécie de
items.example: It was kind of difficult to explain what had happened.
items.note: Informal approximation similar to sort of; not the noun phrase a kind of machine.

items.example: She gave me, like, three different explanations.
items.note: Informal spoken marker for an approximation or hesitation; distinct from the verb like or a formal comparison.

items.pt: enfim; de qualquer forma; seja como for
items.example: Anyway, I should go now, but I will call you later.
items.note: Moves away from a topic, returns to the main point or begins to close the conversation.

items.example: The experiment took longer than expected. Still, the results were useful.
items.note: Expresses a counterpoint or concession, not the time meaning continuing up to now.

items.example: The course is demanding. On the other hand, it offers excellent practical experience.
items.note: Introduces another side of the situation; unlike anyway, the topic remains connected.

items.example: The plan needs attention. I mean, we should review the safety checks first.
items.note: Restates or explains what the speaker intends to say; common in informal conversation.

items.example: My first point is that the project has a realistic budget.
items.note: Pedagogical extension: in informal speech, the source also demonstrates announcing reasons by saying the letters A and B.

sectionsChecked: A: Definitions and introductory well, right and OK
B: Opening, steering, returning to and closing conversations
C: Afterthoughts, hesitation, suggestions and interruption management
D: Explanation, approximation, topic management, contrast, clarification and spoken lettered points

units.title: Unit 68 — Linking words in writing
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 68. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Structure a formal text with sequencing, transitions, summaries and conclusions.
Explain, exemplify and rephrase ideas using linkers appropriate to the register.
Refer backwards and forwards to other sections, pages, and correspondence.
Distinguish lastly from at last and a summary from an ending statement.

items.example: First, we need to define the problem the report will address.
items.note: Introduces the first point of an organised text; firstly and first of all are alternatives.

items.example: Firstly, the study examines the available evidence.
items.note: Formal sequencing expression, often followed by secondly and thirdly.

items.pt: antes de tudo; em primeiro lugar
items.example: First of all, the committee must agree on the objectives.
items.note: Introduces the first item or priority in an explanation.

items.example: Next, we compare the results with those of the previous trial.
items.note: Moves to a subsequent point or step in an ordered argument.

items.example: Secondly, the proposed changes would reduce maintenance costs.
items.note: Marks the second point in a formal list or argument.

items.example: Thirdly, we must consider the impact on local residents.
items.note: Often follows firstly and secondly when structuring successive arguments.

items.example: Finally, the team will present its recommendations to management.
items.note: Can signal the last point in a list; in other contexts, can mean after a long wait.

items.example: Lastly, I would like to thank everyone who reviewed the proposal.
items.note: Introduces the final item in a sequence, not something that eventually happened after a delay.

items.example: At last, the delayed report has arrived.
items.note: Means finally after a long time; do not use it instead of lastly to introduce the final argument.

items.pt: passando a; quanto a; voltando-se para
items.example: Turning to the next question, we should consider the financial risks.
items.note: Marks a deliberate move to a new topic; typically followed by a noun or noun phrase.

items.pt: deixando de lado; sem entrar na questão de
items.example: Leaving aside the cost, the design has several technical advantages.
items.note: Sets a question aside rather than discussing it; usually followed by a noun or noun phrase.

items.pt: entre parênteses; como observação à parte
items.example: In parenthesis, the earlier survey reached a similar result.
items.note: Introduces a secondary point not central to the main argument; relatively formal.

items.example: In summary, the evidence supports three practical changes.
items.note: Brings together the main arguments; not merely a signal that writing has ended.

items.example: To sum up, our tests show that the approach is feasible.
items.note: Summarises key ideas, often near the end of a report or presentation.

items.example: In sum, the benefits appear to outweigh the risks.
items.note: Much more formal than to sum up; expresses the overall substance of the argument.

items.example: In conclusion, I recommend approving the proposal.
items.note: Signals that the text is ending; not always suitable when the writer is specifically summing up preceding arguments.

items.example: To conclude, I would like to identify the next steps.
items.note: A formal signal that the discussion is coming to an end.

items.example: The sensor is unreliable; in other words, it sometimes reports incorrect values.
items.note: Restates an idea more clearly or simply, without necessarily adding a new argument.

items.pt: isto é; quer dizer; ou seja
items.example: The system is redundant; that is to say, another unit can take over if one fails.
items.note: A relatively formal expression for clarifying what has just been said.

items.example: Several materials are suitable; for example, aluminium is easy to machine.
items.note: Introduces one example that illustrates a broader statement.

items.example: Some changes could be immediate; for instance, we could revise the timetable.
items.note: Similar to for example in formal and informal writing.

items.example: We could invite, say, three external experts to review the plan.
items.note: Used parenthetically to suggest an example; commas usually set it off in writing.

items.example: Briefly, the new process has two major stages.
items.note: Signals a short explanation that does not cover every detail.

items.pt: por assim dizer; modo de dizer
items.example: This small change is, so to speak, the missing piece of the puzzle.
items.note: Shows that a phrase is figurative or not completely precise.

items.example: The team is, as it were, building a bridge between research and industry.
items.note: More formal than so to speak; softens a figurative or approximate description.

items.example: The following sections explain the design and its limitations.
items.note: Refers forward to items that will appear immediately afterwards; followed by an appropriate noun or can stand alone.

items.example: The assumptions stated above also apply to the second experiment.
items.note: Above directs a reader to information earlier in the same text.

items.example: As explained earlier, this method depends on accurate timing.
items.note: Points back to a part of the text already presented.

items.pt: veja acima; consulte o trecho anterior
items.example: For the definition of these terms, see above.
items.note: A short written reference to information appearing earlier in a document.

items.example: The detailed measurements are shown in the table; see below.
items.note: Directs the reader to content later in the text; opposite of see above.

items.example: The complete schedule is printed overleaf.
items.note: Directs a reader to the other side of a sheet; especially relevant to printed documents.

items.example: For further details, consult the technical appendix.
items.note: Conventional phrase directing readers to additional information.

items.example: For further discussion, see the final chapter.
items.note: Indicates where readers can find more extensive treatment of an issue.

items.pt: encaminhar você a; remeter você a
items.example: May I refer you to the appendix for a fuller explanation?
items.note: Formal refer someone to a document or location means direct their attention there; target is a short pronounceable verb phrase.

items.pt: em referência a; com relação a
items.example: With reference to your recent email, I can confirm the meeting date.
items.note: Formal opening linking an email or letter to earlier correspondence.

sectionsChecked: A: Formal-text order, topic change, omission, digression, summary and conclusion
A: Common mistake contrasting lastly with at last
B: Explanation, illustration, short account and deliberately imprecise phrasing
C: Backward/forward references, page pointers and earlier correspondence
